title: Faithfulness
hookLine: keep promises to your spouse and your people

lines: WHITHER THOU GOEST, I WILL GO.
cards: On the road out of Moab, three widows stop walking. Naomi, the mother-in-law, tells her two daughters-in-law to go home. She has nothing left to give them.
One, Orpah, kisses her goodbye and turns back. The other, Ruth, won't let go: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Those words aren't spoken between a husband and wife. They're spoken between two women with nothing left but each other. Today: the commandment about adultery, and the larger thing it protects.

teach.b: The commandment itself is short: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." It guards marriage, the promise two people make to belong to each other.
But scripture keeps setting that promise inside a bigger one: God's faithfulness to people who aren't always faithful back.
The prophet Hosea is told to keep loving a wife who leaves him, as a living picture of God's love for a wandering people.
Lamentations, a book of grief over a ruined city, still says: "great is thy faithfulness." And the second letter to Timothy says: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself."
In this reading, faithfulness isn't first a rule about bodies. It's a reflection of who God is.
Jesus takes this commandment inward, the way he did with killing: looking at someone with lust, he says, is already adultery in the heart.
Faithfulness starts where nobody else can see. And its reach goes wider than marriage. Ruth isn't married to Naomi.
She simply won't leave. Friendships, families, congregations and teams all run on kept promises. Churches differ on marriage and divorce.

Catholics and Orthodox Christians understand marriage as a sacrament; the Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, can't be dissolved, while Orthodox churches can allow a second marriage in some cases.
Protestant churches hold a range of views.
Underneath all of them, the commandment asks the same plain thing: when you've given your word, keep it.

how: Christians make vows of faithfulness at weddings, and Ruth's words to Naomi are sometimes read at them; churches teach this commandment as faithfulness in marriage, though Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches differ on divorce and remarriage.

o: believing every teaching of your church without doubt
going to church services every single week
keeping your word to those you've promised, as God does

p: whither thou goest, I will go
keeps loving a wife who leaves

s: Ruth's words were spoken between husband and wife
Ruth says them to Naomi, her mother-in-law, on the road out of Moab.
the second letter to Timothy says God stays faithful even when we don't believe
"If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself."
all churches teach the same about divorce

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and Naomi tells you to go back to your own people. Orpah has already turned back. what do you do?
o: stay with Naomi: thy people shall be my people.
wait in Moab and decide later.
games.why: Ruth won't let go: "whither thou goest, I will go." faithfulness, here, between two widows.

practice: Bring to mind a promise you're keeping halfway, I'll call more, I'll be there, I'll fix that, to a spouse, a friend, a child, a team, and hold it honestly, without excuses and without beating yourself up.
What would keeping it fully look like, in one concrete act? If you pray, you can ask God for help to keep it.

wordCard.voice: Faithfulness. Keeping the promises you've made, to a spouse and to your people, the way scripture says God keeps his.

orig.note: Hebrew: faithfulness, steadiness. The word behind great is thy faithfulness in Lamentations 3:23.

carryVoice: Your line: faithful. That's a week of commandments: no other gods, no idols, the Name, the sabbath, parents, killing, and now faithfulness. Same time tomorrow.
